Oct 6, 2026

## **Fast Finality \+ Networking**

Invited [francesco.damato@ethereum.org](mailto:francesco.damato@ethereum.org) [Sukun Tarachandani](mailto:sukun.tarachandani@ethereum.org) [raul.kripalani@ethereum.org](mailto:raul.kripalani@ethereum.org) [Ben Edgington](mailto:ben.edgington@ethereum.org) [Roberto Saltini](mailto:roberto.saltini@ethereum.org) [Yann Vonlanthen](mailto:yann.vonlanthen@ethereum.org) [Kamil Salakhiev](mailto:kamil.salakhiev@ethereum.org) [francesco@ethlabs.org](mailto:francesco@ethlabs.org) [anton.nashatyrev@consensys.com](mailto:anton.nashatyrev@consensys.com) ~~[mikhail.kalinin@consensys.com](mailto:mikhail.kalinin@consensys.com)~~ ~~[barnabe@ethlabs.org](mailto:barnabe@ethlabs.org)~~

Meeting records [Transcript](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zp2xGqYeftV6g7i7sv8LWM_OVhsn_67_OsfaSCN4tLc/edit?usp=drive_web&tab=t.hciylsnafyr3) 

### **Summary**

Network synchronization and consensus strategies debated and simulation traffic analyzed for Cambridge.

**Finality and Committee Decisions**  
Participants agreed to maintain the current requirement of waiting for finality without adding state-dependency complexities. A simple pseudo-random algorithm was selected for committee rotation.

**Workshop and Simulation Planning**  
Post-quantum cryptography discussions were scheduled for the Cambridge workshop. Devnet targets 16 slots while simulation traffic bottlenecks and node compositions were reviewed.

### **Decisions**

## Needs Further Discussion

* **Target slot count for finality** The team provisionally targeted 16 slots as the best case for finality, subject to revision based on feasibility.

### **Next steps**

- [ ] \[Kamil Salakhiev\] Write up proof propagation: Compose a document detailing proof propagation ideas for presentation at the Cambridge workshop.

- [ ] \[Kamil Salakhiev\] Lead PQ session: Coordinate and lead the Post Quantum session at the Cambridge workshop on Wednesday.

- [ ] \[Sukun Tarachandani, Yann Vonlanthen\] Discuss parameter sizing: Meet today or tomorrow morning to finalize the sizing of different parameters.

- [ ] \[Sukun Tarachandani\] Share simulator results: Post the latest simulator results in the telegram group for team review.

- [ ] \[Anton Nashatyrev, Sukun Tarachandani\] Discuss traffic fixes: Meet tomorrow to discuss potential solutions for the I-have-I-want traffic issues identified in the simulations.

- [ ] \[Sukun Tarachandani\] Update Gossip Queue: Implement a priority queue in the gossip sub module to improve message dissemination across mesh peers.

- [ ] \[Sukun Tarachandani\] Map Validator Distribution: Utilize the collected node data to accurately map validator counts for mainnet simulations.

- [ ] \[Anton Nashatyrev\] Formalize EIP Assumptions: Include documentation in the EIP regarding the assumption that home nodes constitute a minority of the network.

- [ ] \[Yann Vonlanthen, Kamil Salakhiev\] Discuss Distribution Improvements: Collaborate to identify efficient methods for validator anonymization and data mapping.

- [ ] \[Yann Vonlanthen, Sukun Tarachandani\] Schedule Friday Session: Determine via asynchronous communication whether to proceed with the proposed Friday session.

### **Details**

* **Agenda and Meeting Objectives**: Yann Vonlanthen opened the meeting by outlining the discussion agenda, focusing on networking, finality synchronization, and preparation for the upcoming Cambridge event. Yann Vonlanthen proposed aligning on committee rotation, bit list determination, subnetwork design, devnet updates, and simulation work before holding breakout sessions later in the week ([00:00:57](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.r064t7oq6vc4)).

* **Bitfield Mapping and Finalized Block State**: Roberto Saltini presented the current idea for bitfield mapping, which involves adding the latest finalized block to attestations so nodes can use its state to determine a superset of active validators ([00:07:04](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.y0z16ak5e9oe)). Yann Vonlanthen questioned why an older state is not used to avoid potential problems, to which Roberto Saltini responded that older states risk missing validators whose deposits were processed in the meantime, preventing proper aggregation ([00:08:40](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.jtx1hcox1jpi)). Roberto Saltini noted that aggregators would add the finalized block as an anchor point, though edge cases involving race conditions when finality progresses on-chain were raised ([00:07:04](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.y0z16ak5e9oe)) ([00:12:21](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.hhd8r1tipgce)). After further discussion involving Sukun Tarachandani, the participants agreed to maintain the current requirement of waiting for finality without adding unnecessary state-dependency complexities ([00:18:47](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.yv1cclai2jr1)).

* **Committee Rotation Algorithms**: Yann Vonlanthen and Roberto Saltini discussed Francesco's proposal regarding committee rotation and whether modular or pseudo-random algorithms should be used to prevent adversarial bunching. Roberto Saltini argued that adversarial majorities in specific committees are mitigated by the stabilization gadget because late or malicious votes are counted in subsequent rounds regardless of committee membership. Yann Vonlanthen and Roberto Saltini concluded that a simple pseudo-random algorithm is acceptable once the validator set is determined ([00:21:46](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.sjw6aqy6crz5)) ([00:24:53](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.dwzj8841qi9j)).

  ![][image1]

* **Slot and Round Synchronization**: Yann Vonlanthen brought up whether rounds need to be synchronized to slots and epochs, noting Mikhail's suggestion to advance the next height after two-thirds of votes are collected. Roberto Saltini expressed skepticism regarding the benefits of mid-round height progression, noting potential timing conflicts for validators voting at the end of a round ([00:28:15](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.ks8g6k1hdk76)). Roberto Saltini proposed an alternative involving dual fields in the state to allow early finalization targets without advancing height, and the participants agreed to defer this complex topic to a whiteboard session in Cambridge ([00:30:02](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.begrt68mnc51)).

  ![][image2]

* **Cambridge Workshop Planning and Post-Quantum Cryptography**: Ben Edgington proposed organizing post-quantum cryptography discussions into a dedicated session on the third day of Cambridge to avoid continuous distractions from core consensus delivery. Kamil Salakhiev agreed to lead the post-quantum session, present proof propagation ideas discussed with Kev, and review the write-up on sub-multisignatures ([00:37:08](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.9kug5xcbecp6)). Yann Vonlanthen and Kamil Salakhiev coordinated scheduling the session for Wednesday afternoon, ensuring coordination with other workshop tracks and participants like Kevin ([00:38:27](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.l0wv27u2ryo)).

  ![][image3]

* **Finality Targets and Devnet Implementation**: Sukun Tarachandani asked about the target finality slots for the devnet, prompting Ben Edgington to clarify that they are targeting 16 slots (four epochs), which is four times faster than the current best case of 64 slots ([00:41:36](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.y9s7pjxs6xss)). Sukun Tarachandani reported modifying the Prism client code to implement the voting structure presented by Anton Nashatyrev and the committee structure proposed by Yann Vonlanthen, removing latching conditions so finality keeps moving despite simplified fork choice rules ([00:35:37](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.6qmv5h334g8k)) ([00:42:48](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.su2tr8i74h24)). Sukun Tarachandani announced plans to run simulations with a 500-node cluster comparing standard flooding, staggered publishing, and multi-committee scheduling ([00:35:37](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.6qmv5h334g8k)) ([00:45:18](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.kof1odkc0w47)).

* **Simulation Traffic Analysis and I Have/I Want Optimizations**: Anton Nashatyrev shared simulation updates, noting that fixing a connection scaling bug reduced internal traffic to 5% of overall traffic in a simulation of 1,000 nodes and one million validators. Anton Nashatyrev reported working on Snappy compression for attestation and aggregate messages and noted that duplicate requests caused by naive "I have/I want" implementations during slot-start publishing remain a major performance bottleneck ([00:52:33](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.xapk2jv4o0us)) ([00:56:37](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.mw7hru9p57yd)). Sukun Tarachandani confirmed experiencing the same issue with slot-start publishing, and the participants agreed to discuss workarounds suggested by Chaba during their next sync ([00:57:56](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.f7qdwbka66ng)).

* **Gossip Sub Implementation and Attestation Queue Modification**: Sukun Tarachandani proposed replacing the first-in-first-out queue with a priority queue in the gossip sub implementation. The proposed change aims to better distribute attestation messages across mesh peers, such as sending subsets of 10 items out of 100 total attestations to different peers, thereby improving message dissemination. Sukun Tarachandani suggested that they discuss this topic further the following day ([00:59:00](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.nl1k16z81ft2)).

* **Validator Distribution Realism in Simulations**: Kamil Salakhiev raised a question regarding the realism of current simulator assumptions, pointing out that assuming an even distribution where each node runs 1,000 validators (out of 1 million validators and 1,000 nodes) does not reflect real-life conditions ([00:59:00](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.nl1k16z81ft2)). Sukun Tarachandani clarified that in their setup, home nodes run 1 to 3 validators while the remainder are distributed equally among super nodes, and admitted to not yet mapping exact mainnet distributions. Kamil Salakhiev shared that they were working on obtaining accurate mapping numbers as a weekend project using Jan's paper on anonymizing validators and a spread framework attack ([01:00:18](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.z7yyb0htmfl)). Kamil Salakhiev displayed preliminary data from a simulation involving approximately 13,000 validators and asked whether super nodes should be assigned higher bandwidth capabilities ([01:01:16](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.xba47chmgfv3)).

  ![][image4]

* **Network Node Composition and Bandwidth Assumptions**: Anton Nashatyrev and Sukun Tarachandani discussed network node composition and capacity assumptions for their simulations ([01:02:27](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.79o06uauzppb)). Anton Nashatyrev stated that their simulation utilizes a few huge super nodes and a majority of virtual private server nodes with bandwidths of a few hundred megabits, treating home nodes as a minority of 5% to 10%. In contrast, Sukun Tarachandani reported that their simulation uses 20% super nodes and 80% home nodes, where home nodes represent the majority of beacon nodes but most validators reside on super nodes ([01:03:32](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.r5i8bcoek5b3)). Sukun Tarachandani noted that reverse-lookup data from sharding results indicates 40% to 50% cloud nodes, which may serve as a more accurate baseline. Anton Nashatyrev suggested formalizing these capacity assumptions in an Ethereum Improvement Proposal because the network might fail under a majority of low-bandwidth home nodes, whereas Sukun Tarachandani countered that average ISPs commonly provide around 100 megabits ([01:04:55](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.37o1m6vyf4y)). Additionally, Yann Vonlanthen offered to chat with Kamil Salakhiev offline to help simplify the validator anonymization follow-ups ([01:06:32](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.um8sn2mf7pdz)).

* **Meeting Wrap-Up and Future Sessions**: Yann Vonlanthen reviewed the agenda, noted that all topics had been covered, and mentioned a potential Friday session with Sukun Tarachandani to be coordinated offline or in Cambridge due to travel schedules. Yann Vonlanthen highlighted that at least two breakout sessions were already scheduled for Cambridge before the meeting concluded with farewells from Yann Vonlanthen, Roberto Saltini, Anton Nashatyrev, Sukun Tarachandani, and Kamil Salakhiev ([01:06:32](?tab=t.hciylsnafyr3#heading=h.um8sn2mf7pdz)).
